# Exercise 1.1 — Two languages, one analysis {#sec-two-languages}

**45 minutes · work in pairs, one of you driving each language**

:::: {.web-only}
Everything on this page runs in your browser. The first cell you run takes a
little while to start — it is downloading R or Python itself — and everything
after that is immediate.
::::

## Objectives

::: {.objective-list}
- Read a `.csv`, filter rows, summarise by group, fit a linear model and draw a
  scatter plot, in either language, without a cheat sheet open.
- Point at a number in your output and say whether it would be identical in the
  other language, and why.
:::

## Why both

R and Python encode two different ideas of what an analysis *is*. In R the unit
is the data frame and the verbs act on whole columns; in Python the unit is the
object and you call methods on it. Most differences you meet today follow from
that one difference.

## Load and look

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
library(readr)
los <- read_csv("data/los_data.csv")
head(los)
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
import pandas as pd
los = pd.read_csv("data/los_data.csv")
los.info()
```
:::

A difference worth noticing immediately: `read_csv()` guesses column types and
*tells you what it guessed*; `pd.read_csv()` guesses and says nothing. A column
of ages containing one entry of `"unknown"` becomes `character` in R, with a
message, and `object` in pandas, in silence.

## Filter, and summarise by group

This is where the two look least alike.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
library(dplyr)
los |>
  mutate(sev_band = if_else(Severity > 7, "high", "low")) |>
  group_by(sev_band) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_los = mean(LOS), .groups = "drop")
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
(los
 .assign(sev_band=lambda d: (d["Severity"] > 7).map({True: "high", False: "low"}))
 .groupby("sev_band")["LOS"]
 .agg(n="size", mean_los="mean")
 .reset_index())
```
:::

## Fit a linear model

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
fit_r <- lm(LOS ~ Age + Severity, data = los)
coef(fit_r)
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
X = los[["Age", "Severity"]]     # 2-D: a frame, not a series
y = los["LOS"]                   # 1-D
fit_py = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
fit_py.intercept_, fit_py.coef_
```
:::

Two things differ here and only one matters. `lm()` returns a statistical
summary — standard errors, residuals, an F test — because R's linear model was
written for inference; `LinearRegression` returns coefficients and a
`.predict()` method, because scikit-learn's was written for prediction. That is
a difference in purpose. The coefficients themselves agree to every decimal you
care to print, because both solve the same least-squares problem on the same
rows. That is not a difference at all.

## Draw it

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(los, aes(x = Age, y = LOS)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Length of stay (days)")
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(los["Age"], los["LOS"], alpha=0.3)
ax.set_xlabel("Age (years)"); ax.set_ylabel("Length of stay (days)")
plt.show()
```
:::

## Task 1 — The idiom table

Fill in the missing cells. Guess from the examples above before looking
anything up.

| Operation | R (tidyverse) | Python (pandas) |
|---|---|---|
| keep some rows | `filter(Age > 65)` | `df[df["Age"] > 65]` |
| keep some columns | `select(Age, LOS)` | ? |
| make a new column | `mutate(z = Age / 10)` | ? |
| sort | ? | `df.sort_values("LOS")` |
| count by group | `count(sev_band)` | ? |
| first six rows | `head(los)` | ? |
| number of rows | `nrow(los)` | ? |

: {tbl-colwidths="[28,36,36]"}

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Every answer is one tidyverse verb or one DataFrame method: `arrange()`,
`df.assign()`, `df.value_counts()`, `df.head()`, `len(df)`.
:::

## Task 2 — The same number, twice

Compute the mean length of stay among patients with `Severity` above 7, in both
languages. Replace each `______`.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{webr}
#| exercise: mean_high_r
source("checks/checks.R")
mean_los_high <- los |> filter(______) |> pull(LOS) |> ______
check_metric_range(mean_los_high, 70, 100, "mean LOS, high severity")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: mean_high_r
#| solution: true
source("checks/checks.R")
mean_los_high <- los |> filter(Severity > 7) |> pull(LOS) |> mean()
check_metric_range(mean_los_high, 70, 100, "mean LOS, high severity")
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: mean_high_py
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
mean_los_high = los.loc[______, "LOS"].______
check_metric_range(mean_los_high, 70, 100, "mean LOS, high severity")
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: mean_high_py
#| solution: true
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
mean_los_high = los.loc[los["Severity"] > 7, "LOS"].mean()
check_metric_range(mean_los_high, 70, 100, "mean LOS, high severity")
```
:::

The two should agree exactly — same rows, same arithmetic. If they do not, you
have filtered differently, and the usual cause is `>` against `>=`.

## Task 3 — Put the model on the plot

Add the fitted values from the **two-predictor** model to a scatter of LOS
against age. This is not the same as the `geom_smooth()` line above, which fits
`LOS ~ Age` alone and ignores severity — and the difference is the point of the
task.

```{webr}
#| exercise: plot_fitted
los$fitted <- ______
ggplot(los, aes(x = Age)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = LOS), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(y = fitted), colour = "red", size = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Length of stay (days)")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: plot_fitted
#| hint: true
# `fit_r` is already fitted. You want its predictions for every row.
los$fitted <- predict(______)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: plot_fitted
#| solution: true
los$fitted <- predict(fit_r)
ggplot(los, aes(x = Age)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = LOS), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(y = fitted), colour = "red", size = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Length of stay (days)")
```

The fitted values do not fall on a single line against age. Why not? Your answer
to that is worth more than the plot.

## Task 4 — Find a difference that matters

Between you, find **one** place where the two languages genuinely give different
results for the same instruction, and one where they only appear to. A sentence
each. Somewhere to start: random number generation, how each handles a missing
value inside `mean()`, and what happens when you index a frame with a number.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Model answers.** *Genuinely different*: the random number streams —
`set.seed(42)` and `random_state=42` select different rows, so any split,
bootstrap or shuffle differs between languages. This is the one that bites in
1.2, and it is worth saying in plenary. Also genuine: `mean()` on a vector
containing `NA` returns `NA` in R, while pandas `.mean()` skips missing values,
so the same instruction gives a number in one language and a refusal in the
other. *Only apparently different*: the regression coefficients (identical least
squares), `nrow()` against `len()`, and 0- against 1-based indexing, which
changes the code you type but not the rows you get.

**If a pair finishes early**, ask which language's default for missing values
they would prefer in a clinical audit, and to defend it. There is no right
answer; there is a right standard of argument.
:::
:::

## Stretch

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 1 — parsnip, so that 1.2 feels familiar
Refit with `parsnip`, the part of `tidymodels` that standardises model fitting:
`linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm") |> fit(LOS ~ Age + Severity, data = los)`.
The coefficients are identical, because `set_engine("lm")` means it is calling
`lm()`. What `tidymodels` adds is one interface in front of many engines, which
is what makes the pipeline in 1.2 swappable.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — Make the same split in both languages
Draw an 80/20 split in R, write the row indices out, and reproduce the identical
split in Python. This is tedious, and that is the lesson: cross-language
reproducibility is not free, and the professional answer is to split once, in
one language, and save the result.
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that you can perform the five basic operations in both languages, and
that the coefficients you obtained are a property of the data rather than of the
software.

**Cannot:** anything about how well this model predicts. Every number here was
computed on the same 1000 rows the model was fitted to. That is @sec-pipeline.
